primitives.name: Hearing Communication Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: First among these, as we have said, is the fact that hearing is not only a sense of communication, but a sense of communication which receives its chief use in establishing a rapport with other individuals.
primitives.assumptions: Hearing is fundamentally tied to interpersonal communication; non-speech auditory inputs are secondary.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When hearing is isolated from speech feedback, communication efficacy degrades.

layer2.mapping: The kernel maps acoustic input to communicative intent via feedback-controlled speech synthesis.
layer2.telemetry: Speech intelligibility index under varying auditory feedback conditions.

primitives.name: Speech Perception Feedback Loop
primitives.verbatim_quote: We see that the processes of speech and hearing in the normal person have never been separated; but that the very learning of speech has been conditioned by the fact that each individual hears himself speak.
primitives.assumptions: Speech acquisition requires concurrent auditory self-monitoring.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Disruption of auditory feedback leads to degraded speech production quality.

layer2.mapping: Feedback loop enables real-time correction of speech output based on perceived output.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that hearing is not merely a passive receptor of sound but an active component of communication and speech development. The kernel of this relationship lies in the interdependence of auditory perception and vocal production—where one cannot be fully understood without the other. This duality implies a closed-loop system where feedback from self-generated speech informs perception, and vice versa. The failure mode arises when this loop is disrupted, such as in deafness or auditory prosthetics that lack real-time feedback. The mathematical structure reflects a dynamic system where R(t) = f(H(t), S(t)) defines rapport as a function of hearing and speech parameters. The feedback loop is modeled as E(t) = |S_{in}(t) - S_{out}(t)|, where error decreases with improved auditory monitoring. Prosthetic design must therefore optimize I_eff(B,A) to maintain effective communication despite sensory loss.
